difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring recognition of a self-selection confound: patients who seek out experimental treatments differ systematically from the general patient population. Distractors plausibly address one horn only.
stimulus: Patients who voluntarily enroll in experimental cancer drug trials at a major research hospital have a 20 percent higher five-year survival rate than patients treated with standard therapies at the same hospital. Yet when the hospital made the experimental drug available to all cancer patients as a standard treatment, overall five-year survival rates did not improve.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental drug was significantly more expensive to administer than the standard therapies it was intended to replace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only patients whose cancer was detected at an early stage were eligible to enroll in the experimental drug trials.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some patients declined the experimental drug even after it became available as a standard treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The research hospital had a larger oncology staff than most comparable institutions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who enrolled in experimental trials were more likely to comply with their full course of treatment than those who did not.

explanations.correct: If only early-stage patients were eligible for the trials, the trial group was systematically healthier from the outset, explaining their higher survival rate without any contribution from the drug itself. When the drug was extended to all patients — including late-stage — the survival benefit disappeared because the drug was never the cause of the difference.
explanations.A: Cost explains a potential barrier to access but doesn't account for why broader availability produced no survival improvement; it also doesn't explain the original higher survival rate.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a selection-effect resolution: the trial group was restricted to early-stage patients who had inherently better prognoses, dissolving the apparent contradiction.
explanations.C: Patients declining the drug addresses uptake but leaves unexplained why the original trial group fared so much better; it resolves one horn at most.
explanations.D: Staff size is irrelevant to the comparison between the trial group and the general patient population.
explanations.E: Compliance differences explain the trial group's better outcomes through behavior, not the drug — this deepens the paradox by suggesting the drug still isn't responsible, but it doesn't explain why universal access failed to improve rates if compliance is spread across the broader group.

difficultyReason: Reverse-causation paradox in economics. The apparent conflict — raising the minimum wage correlates with lower teen unemployment — requires identifying a confounding economic trend rather than accepting the surface causal story. Distractors include one that deepens the paradox.
stimulus: Economic analysts expected that cities raising their minimum wage above the national level would see an increase in teen unemployment, since employers would hire fewer low-skilled workers. However, in cities that enacted such raises, teen unemployment rates actually fell in the two years following the wage increase.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Teen workers in cities with higher minimum wages reported greater job satisfaction than those in cities with lower wages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cities that enacted minimum wage increases were those already experiencing robust economic growth and falling unemployment across all age groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Employers in high-minimum-wage cities invested more heavily in automation than employers in other cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national minimum wage was itself raised during the same two-year period in which the city-level raises took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teen workers are more likely than adult workers to be employed in industries directly affected by minimum wage legislation.

explanations.correct: If only already-booming cities chose to raise the minimum wage, the decline in teen unemployment reflects the pre-existing economic expansion, not the wage increase. This confounding variable dissolves the paradox by revealing a selection effect at the policy level.
explanations.A: Job satisfaction does not explain employment rates and addresses neither horn of the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a classic confounding-variable resolution: cities that raised wages were those with strong economies, so falling unemployment tracks economic growth, not wage policy.
explanations.C: Greater automation would predict more unemployment, not less — this deepens the paradox.
explanations.D: A national wage increase affects all cities equally and therefore cannot explain why only the cities that enacted local raises saw the decline.
explanations.E: This confirms teens are affected by minimum wage laws but does not explain why unemployment fell rather than rose; it addresses why teens are relevant, not the direction of the effect.

difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox involving a temporal/contextual difference. The conflict between local air quality improvement and worsening regional air quality is non-obvious; correct answer introduces a displacement mechanism.
stimulus: After a major industrial city installed new emission-control filters at its largest factories, measured air pollution levels within the city dropped by 30 percent over three years. Yet regional air quality monitors located 50 to 100 kilometers downwind of the city recorded a corresponding increase in particulate pollution over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The emission-control filters were more effective at removing certain pollutants than others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regional air quality monitors use a different measurement scale than the city's own monitoring stations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The filters trap particulates within dense filtration media that must be transported to and processed at facilities located downwind of the city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several smaller cities in the region also increased industrial output during the same three-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of the industrial city reported measurable improvements in respiratory health following the installation of the filters.

explanations.correct: If the filters concentrate pollutants that are then transported to processing facilities downwind, the pollution is not eliminated but physically relocated. This explains both the city's cleaner air and the region's dirtier air through a single hidden mechanism — a displacement effect.
explanations.A: Selective effectiveness explains partial improvement within the city but does not account for the increase downwind; resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: A measurement-scale difference could explain why the numbers look different, but a 'corresponding increase' implies the regional monitors are calibrated — this is too vague to resolve the paradox and functions as an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.C: Correct. The pollution is displaced, not destroyed — the filter medium is transported downwind, introducing a hidden causal pathway that reconciles both observations.
explanations.D: Other cities' industrial growth could explain regional pollution increases independently, but it doesn't connect to the city's filter installation or explain the correspondence in timing; this resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Health improvements corroborate the city's lower pollution but do nothing to explain the regional increase; this is irrelevant to resolving the paradox.

difficultyReason: Law/policy paradox with a definitional mismatch as the resolution. Students must recognize that the same term ('recidivism') is being measured differently across the two data sets, not that one data set is wrong.
stimulus: A state department of corrections reports that prisoners who complete an in-prison vocational training program are 40 percent less likely to be reincarcerated within five years of release than prisoners who do not complete such a program. Yet independent criminologists studying the same prison system found that the vocational training program had no statistically significant effect on recidivism.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vocational training program costs the state significantly less per participant than alternative rehabilitation programs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The department of corrections measures recidivism only as reincarceration, while the criminologists' study counted any subsequent arrest — including those not resulting in conviction — as recidivism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prisoners who completed the vocational program were more likely to find employment within six months of release.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The criminologists studied a different five-year period than the one covered by the department's report.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Not all prisoners who began the vocational training program completed it within their sentence term.

explanations.correct: If the department counts only reincarceration while criminologists count any arrest, the two studies are measuring different outcomes. The program may genuinely reduce reincarceration (perhaps graduates evade reimprisonment even when rearrested) while not reducing arrests overall. This definitional mismatch dissolves the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: Program cost is entirely irrelevant to the discrepancy in recidivism findings.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a definitional/measurement-artifact resolution: the same word 'recidivism' refers to different phenomena in the two reports, explaining why outcomes diverge.
explanations.C: Employment outcomes might explain how the program reduces reincarceration, but this simply corroborates one horn of the paradox without addressing why the criminologists found no effect; resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: A different time period could introduce historical variation, but without knowing how conditions differed it does not specifically resolve the conflict; functions as an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.E: Non-completion rates explain why the program's effect might be diluted but don't account for the sharp divergence in findings across two measurement systems.

difficultyReason: Technology paradox involving reverse causation. The paradox — better safety software correlates with more reported data breaches — is counterintuitive; the resolution requires recognizing that detection, not incidence, drives reporting.
stimulus: Companies that have adopted the latest generation of cybersecurity software report, on average, three times as many data breaches per year as companies still using older security systems. Yet cybersecurity experts maintain that the newer software provides substantially stronger protection against unauthorized data access.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The newer cybersecurity software is considerably more expensive than older systems, limiting its adoption to larger companies with more data to protect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The newer software includes advanced breach-detection and logging tools that identify and record intrusion attempts that older systems would have failed to detect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies using newer security systems tend to operate in industries with stricter regulatory requirements for breach disclosure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cybercriminals frequently target companies known to hold large volumes of sensitive financial data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cybersecurity experts who recommend the newer software are sometimes employed by the companies that manufacture it.

explanations.correct: If the newer software detects breaches that older systems miss entirely, then higher reported breach counts reflect superior detection capability rather than worse security. The actual incidence of unauthorized access may be lower; only measured reports are higher. This measurement-artifact resolution dissolves the paradox.
explanations.A: Size and data volume explain why larger companies might be more targeted but don't account for why better software correlates with more reported breaches; resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. The newer software produces more breach reports because it detects more, not because it protects less — a measurement artifact that reconciles both facts.
explanations.C: Stricter disclosure requirements could contribute to higher reported numbers, but this is a weaker explanation than B because it doesn't address whether actual breaches are higher or lower; functions as a partial/one-horn resolution.
explanations.D: Targeting explains why certain companies are attacked more but does not explain the correlation with software generation specifically.
explanations.E: Expert bias undermines the experts' claims but doesn't resolve the statistical discrepancy; this is an irrelevant distractor that attacks a source rather than the data.

difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox with a temporal-scope resolution. The conflict between a language losing native speakers and gaining overall speakers requires recognizing the distinction between native and second-language acquisition.
stimulus: Linguists studying Catalan have documented a steady decline in the number of people who speak Catalan as their first language over the past three decades. Yet census data from the same period show that the total number of Catalan speakers — including those who learned it later in life — has increased by over 30 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several regional governments have funded Catalan-language broadcasting and media over the past three decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The decline in native Catalan speakers is concentrated among elderly populations in rural communities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government education policies introduced Catalan as a compulsory subject in schools, producing a large cohort of fluent second-language speakers who outnumber the native-speaker losses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many linguists consider second-language speakers to be less proficient in Catalan than native speakers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The region where Catalan is spoken experienced significant population growth due to immigration over the past three decades.

explanations.correct: Compulsory school instruction created a large pool of second-language speakers whose numbers exceed native-speaker losses. This introduces a confounding category — second-language learners — that explains how total speakers can rise even as native speakers decline, resolving both horns simultaneously.
explanations.A: Media funding may encourage learning but doesn't specify a mechanism large enough to explain a 30 percent increase in total speakers; too vague to fully resolve the paradox.
explanations.B: Geographic concentration of native-speaker decline explains where but not why total speakers rose; resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Correct. Mandatory school instruction generates a large, quantifiable second-language cohort that accounts for the numerical increase despite native-speaker loss — a hidden-category resolution.
explanations.D: Proficiency distinctions are irrelevant to the speaker-count discrepancy; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.E: Population growth through immigration could add speakers of other languages but doesn't specifically explain the increase in Catalan speakers unless immigrants learned Catalan — too speculative to fully resolve the paradox.

difficultyReason: History/policy paradox requiring a contextual-difference resolution. The conflict — a tax cut producing more revenue — is the classic supply-side paradox; the resolution requires identifying a behavioral mechanism that increases the tax base, not just the rate.
stimulus: When a European nation reduced its top marginal income tax rate from 75 percent to 45 percent in the early 1980s, the government's total income tax revenue increased substantially over the following decade. Critics had predicted that the rate reduction would cause a significant decline in revenue.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent conflict between the critics' prediction and the actual outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The government simultaneously increased tax rates on corporate profits to offset the income tax reduction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: High-income earners who had previously sheltered income in tax havens abroad repatriated substantial funds once the domestic rate fell below the effective rate of concealment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reduction in the top marginal rate was politically popular and helped the incumbent government win reelection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several neighboring countries also reduced their top marginal tax rates during the same decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government spending on social programs increased substantially during the decade following the tax cut.

explanations.correct: If wealthy taxpayers previously hid income offshore and the lower rate made domestic taxation cheaper than concealment, taxable income expanded dramatically. The tax base grew enough to offset the rate reduction, producing higher total revenue. This behavioral mechanism — increased tax-base participation — dissolves the apparent paradox.
explanations.A: A compensating corporate tax increase would explain stable total revenue through a different revenue stream, not through income tax specifically; this resolves the paradox through a different mechanism than the one described but attributes the gain to a different tax, making it only a partial explanation.
explanations.B: Correct. Repatriation of sheltered income expands the taxable base sufficiently to increase total income tax revenue despite the lower rate — a confounding behavioral-response mechanism.
explanations.C: Political popularity is entirely irrelevant to the revenue outcome; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.D: Neighboring countries' rate reductions provide context but don't explain why this nation's revenue rose; irrelevant distractor.
explanations.E: Increased spending is a government decision orthogonal to revenue; it deepens concern about fiscal balance but doesn't explain the revenue increase.

difficultyReason: Arts/policy paradox with a selection-effect resolution. The conflict — attendance subsidies reduce average audience satisfaction scores — is counterintuitive; resolution requires identifying a compositional change in the audience population.
stimulus: A metropolitan opera company introduced a ticket subsidy program that reduced seat prices by 60 percent for low-income patrons. Following the program's introduction, the opera company's post-performance audience satisfaction surveys showed a statistically significant decline in average satisfaction scores compared to pre-subsidy surveys.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The opera company reduced its production budget in the same season it introduced the subsidy program.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low-income patrons who attended under the subsidy program were attending opera for the first time and were unfamiliar with conventions such as not applauding between movements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The satisfaction surveys were completed voluntarily, and before the subsidy program, only the most enthusiastic attendees — those with the highest baseline satisfaction — chose to complete them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several prominent critics gave the opera company's productions negative reviews during the subsidy period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The subsidy program was funded by a government arts grant that required the opera company to serve a minimum number of low-income patrons per season.

explanations.correct: If pre-subsidy surveys were completed only by the most devoted — and therefore most satisfied — audience members, the baseline scores were inflated by self-selection. The subsidy brought in a broader audience, more of whom completed surveys, diluting the average with more representative, and lower, satisfaction scores. The program didn't cause dissatisfaction; it changed who responded.
explanations.A: A reduced production budget could lower quality and thus satisfaction, explaining the score decline without reference to the subsidy program's audience change — this resolves one horn only and doesn't engage the paradox's full structure.
explanations.B: First-time attendees' unfamiliarity with conventions might explain behavioral issues but doesn't resolve the survey-score paradox; it merely attributes dissatisfaction to newcomers without explaining the measurement artifact.
explanations.C: Correct. Pre-subsidy surveys were completed by a self-selected, highly satisfied subset; post-subsidy surveys captured a broader population, lowering the measured average. This is a classic self-selection/measurement-artifact resolution.
explanations.D: Negative critical reviews might influence audience perceptions but are too indirect and unrelated to the subsidy mechanism to fully resolve the paradox.
explanations.E: The funding mechanism and grant requirements are irrelevant to why satisfaction scores fell; this is an irrelevant distractor.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox involving a reverse-causation mechanism. The conflict — mandatory ethics training correlating with more violations — requires distinguishing increased detection from increased incidence.
stimulus: After a large financial firm made ethics and compliance training mandatory for all employees, the number of internal ethics violations reported to the firm's compliance office rose by 45 percent in the first year. Yet the firm's external auditors found no evidence of an increase in actual unethical conduct during the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ethics training modules were developed by the same compliance office that receives and records reported violations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mandatory training sessions informed employees about the types of conduct that qualify as ethics violations and encouraged them to report suspected misconduct, increasing both awareness and willingness to report.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several employees who completed the mandatory training subsequently left the firm to work for competitors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The compliance office hired additional staff in the year following the training mandate to handle the expected increase in reports.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Financial firms in the same sector that did not adopt mandatory ethics training saw their violation rates remain stable during the same period.

explanations.correct: Training both taught employees what counts as a violation and encouraged reporting. Pre-training, many violations went unreported because employees didn't recognize them or feared reporting. Post-training, more violations were reported even though actual unethical conduct was unchanged — exactly what the auditors confirmed. Increased reporting reflects better awareness and reporting culture, not more misconduct.
explanations.A: The compliance office developing its own training might raise questions of bias but doesn't explain the discrepancy between reported violations and actual conduct; irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. Training increased both definitional awareness and reporting propensity, causing reports to rise while actual violations stayed flat — a detection-versus-incidence resolution.
explanations.C: Employee departures are irrelevant to the violation reporting rate; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.D: Hiring additional compliance staff might facilitate processing more reports, but if violations were truly rising, auditors would have found evidence — this doesn't explain the auditors' finding and resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Stable rates elsewhere highlight the correlation but don't explain the mechanism; this is an irrelevant comparison that leaves the paradox unresolved.

difficultyReason: Environmental science/economics paradox requiring a temporal-scope distinction. Higher fuel efficiency standards correlating with higher total fuel consumption is counterintuitive; the resolution involves a behavioral rebound effect that students must identify.
stimulus: In a large industrialized country, government regulations requiring significantly higher fuel efficiency in new automobiles were enacted fifteen years ago. Yet total national gasoline consumption has increased by 18 percent since those regulations took effect, despite the fact that the average fuel efficiency of vehicles on the road has improved substantially.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fuel efficiency regulations apply only to new vehicles, and many households continue to drive older, less efficient cars purchased before the regulations took effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fuel efficiency regulations were opposed by automobile manufacturers at the time of their enactment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because more fuel-efficient vehicles cost less to operate per kilometer, drivers have increased the total number of kilometers they drive each year, more than offsetting the per-kilometer fuel savings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The country's population increased by 12 percent during the fifteen years since the regulations took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hybrid and electric vehicles, which consume little or no gasoline, have become more widely available since the regulations were enacted.

explanations.correct: This is the classic rebound effect: lower per-kilometer costs induced by greater efficiency cause drivers to drive more total kilometers, increasing absolute fuel consumption even as consumption per kilometer falls. The behavioral response to cheaper driving offsets and exceeds the efficiency gains, resolving both horns of the paradox.
explanations.A: Older vehicles still on the road could limit the efficiency improvement's impact, but the stimulus stipulates that average efficiency has improved substantially — this resolves one horn only and contradicts the premise slightly.
explanations.B: Manufacturer opposition is entirely irrelevant to consumption outcomes; this is an irrelevant distractor.
explanations.C: Correct. The rebound effect — increased driving due to lower per-kilometer cost — explains how total fuel use rises even as per-vehicle efficiency improves; a behavioral confounding mechanism.
explanations.D: A 12 percent population increase could contribute to higher consumption, but a larger population of more efficient drivers should still consume less per capita — this only partially resolves the paradox and does not account for the full 18 percent increase given the efficiency improvements.
explanations.E: Wider availability of electric vehicles would predict lower gasoline consumption, not higher — this deepens the paradox rather than resolving it.
